interactions.label: In a leprosy skin lesion, sensory modalities are lost in a characteristic sequen

params.question: In a leprosy skin lesion, sensory modalities are lost in a characteristic sequence. Which modality is lost first?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Temperature sensation is lost first because the unmyelinated C-fibres carrying thermal input are most susceptible to damage by Mycobacterium leprae. The sequence is temperature → pain → light touch.
Incorrect. Pain sensation is the second modality to be lost. Temperature goes first — reflecting early C-fibre involvement — followed by pain, and finally light touch.
Incorrect. Light touch is the last modality to be lost in a leprosy lesion, as it is carried by larger, more resistant fibres. The correct order is temperature → pain → light touch.
Incorrect. Vibration sense is carried by large myelinated fibres and is not part of the classical sensory loss sequence in leprosy. The order involves temperature → pain → light touch.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct order is temperature → pain → light touch. Temperature is lost first because the unmyelinated C-fibres are most vulnerable to M. leprae–induced nerve damage.
Well done. This sequence — temperature first, then pain, then light touch — helps you detect leprosy early, when only thermal sense is impaired over the lesion.

interactions.label: A negative slit-skin smear definitively rules out a diagnosis of leprosy.

params.question: A negative slit-skin smear definitively rules out a diagnosis of leprosy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect — the statement is false. A negative smear never rules out leprosy. Paucibacillary patients are smear-negative by definition because their strong immunity limits bacterial multiplication below detectable levels. The WHO allows diagnosis and treatment initiation based on clinical signs alone.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Paucibacillary patients have strong cell-mediated immunity that keeps the bacterial load below the smear detection threshold, making them smear-negative by definition. An anaesthetic patch alone is a WHO cardinal sign sufficient for diagnosis.

interactions.label: Why must nerve-function assessment be performed at every follow-up visit in a le

params.question: Why must nerve-function assessment be performed at every follow-up visit in a leprosy patient, even when the patient reports no new complaints?

answers.text: To document nerve thickening for medicolegal records

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The primary clinical reason is to detect silent neuropathy — progressive nerve damage that occurs without pain or visible skin changes and is only found by active sensory and motor testing at each visit.

answers.text: Because silent neuropathy causes progressive nerve damage without any symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Silent neuropathy is painless, progressive loss of nerve function that the patient cannot detect. Only active testing at each visit catches it early enough for corticosteroid rescue, preventing permanent deformity. Borderline (BT, BB, BL) patients carry the highest risk.

answers.text: To determine when multidrug therapy can be safely stopped

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. MDT duration is set by the number of supervised monthly doses completed, not by nerve-function findings. Repeat nerve exams are done to detect silent neuropathy — nerve damage that needs urgent corticosteroid treatment.

answers.text: Because nerve-function loss in leprosy is always painful, and patients may underreport pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The opposite is true — silent neuropathy is defined by the ABSENCE of pain or symptoms. The nerve deteriorates silently, which is precisely why active testing at every visit is mandatory.

overallFeedback.feedback: Silent neuropathy causes painless, progressive nerve-function loss that the patient will not notice or report. Only active testing at every follow-up visit can detect it while corticosteroid rescue is still possible.
Well done. Silent neuropathy is a critical concept — the patient feels nothing while nerve function declines. Early detection with corticosteroids can still rescue the nerve.

interactions.label: A patient on multibacillary MDT develops crops of painful tender subcutaneous no

params.question: A patient on multibacillary MDT develops crops of painful tender subcutaneous nodules with fever and joint pain, consistent with severe erythema nodosum leprosum. What is the correct management?

answers.text: Discontinue MDT and start prednisolone until the reaction subsides

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. MDT must NEVER be stopped during a lepra reaction. The reaction is an immune response, not a sign of treatment failure — stopping MDT risks disease progression without resolving the reaction.

answers.text: Continue MDT and add prednisolone or high-dose clofazimine (300 mg/day)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. MDT continues throughout. For severe ENL, prednisolone or high-dose clofazimine (300 mg/day for 1–3 months, then tapered) is added. Note the dosing distinction: the anti-inflammatory dose (300 mg/day) is six times the standard MDT dose (50 mg/day).

answers.text: Replace clofazimine with thalidomide as the first-line treatment for all patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Although thalidomide is highly effective for severe or recurrent ENL, it is an absolute teratogen and reserved exclusively for men and post-menopausal women. Prednisolone or high-dose clofazimine is the standard first-line approach.

answers.text: Stop clofazimine and increase the dapsone dose to compensate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Stopping any MDT component during a reaction is wrong. Clofazimine is not replaced — its dose is INCREASED to 300 mg/day as an anti-inflammatory measure while all other MDT drugs continue unchanged.

overallFeedback.feedback: MDT must continue through any lepra reaction. For severe ENL, add prednisolone or high-dose clofazimine (300 mg/day). Thalidomide is effective but restricted to men and post-menopausal women due to absolute teratogenicity.

Correct. Two rules never bend during a lepra reaction: continue MDT throughout, and never give thalidomide to a woman of childbearing potential. The clofazimine anti-inflammatory dose (300 mg/day) is a frequent exam question.

interactions.label: A patient has only two hypopigmented patches on his trunk, but the slit-skin sme

params.question: A patient has only two hypopigmented patches on his trunk, but the slit-skin smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli. Which treatment regimen is appropriate?

answers.text: Paucibacillary MDT (rifampicin + dapsone) for 6 months, since the lesion count is low

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Lesion count does not determine the regimen when a smear result is available. A positive smear at any site classifies the patient as multibacillary, requiring the three-drug, 12-month regimen regardless of how few lesions are present.

answers.text: Extended paucibacillary MDT for 9 months with added clofazimine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no 'extended PB-MDT' regimen in the WHO guidelines. A positive smear overrides the lesion count and places the patient firmly in the multibacillary category, needing the standard 12-month three-drug course.

answers.text: Dapsone monotherapy with monthly monitoring of smear status

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Dapsone monotherapy was the pre-MDT era approach and is no longer recommended. A smear-positive patient needs multibacillary MDT: rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone for 12 months.

Correct. A positive slit-skin smear at any site classifies the patient as multibacillary. The regimen is rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + clofazimine 300 mg monthly (supervised) and 50 mg daily + dapsone 100 mg daily, for 12 months.

overallFeedback.feedback: A positive slit-skin smear overrides the lesion count. This patient is multibacillary and needs rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone for 12 months.
Exactly right. A positive smear means multibacillary disease — the full three-drug, 12-month course — no matter how few lesions are visible. This is a key prescribing rule.
